finding: The live range of $160-$875 is about right at the bottom and too high at the top for the four vehicles checked; it is too wide. Built totals, parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr (the national middle labor rate used for these checks), with no coolant: economy 2015 Corolla about $134-$205 (0.9-1.0 hr); midsize 2016 Camry 2.5L about $126-$242 (0.9-1.3 hr); truck 2016 F-150 5.0L about $138-$363 (1.0-2.0 hr); luxury 2015 BMW 328i about $210-$497 (1.0-2.0 hr). The bottom: our lowest totals ($126-$138) pair an online aftermarket thermostat with a manufacturer warranty time and leave out the gasket and the coolant that every thermostat job needs, so $160 is a fair floor for a real quote. The top: the highest total we can build is about $497, for a genuine BMW thermostat assembly at list plus 2 hours, and the highest published benchmark is $747 (Kelley Blue Book), so $875 is above everything found. The evidence that the job can run higher is real but narrow: GM allows 1.9 hr for the thermostat housing on 2021 V6 crossovers because the intake manifold comes off, Ford's 3.5L F-150 uses a $205 thermostat-and-outlet unit, and Acura allows 4.1 hr on the NSX. A ceiling near $750 would cover those cases and match the benchmarks. Our mainstream totals sit far below RepairPal ($616-$716) and Kelley Blue Book ($661-$747), and the gap is almost entirely parts: RepairPal assumes $421-$429 and RepairSmith $350-$400, while the thermostat for these four vehicles costs $18-$177 even at dealer list. We could not find a parts price that supports those figures on a plain thermostat; they fit cars with an integrated electronic thermostat housing, or quotes that fold in coolant and a flush. How solid the labor times are: economy rests on a Hyundai warranty time for a 2017 Elantra (0.9 hr) and one mechanic's 'about 1 hour' for an older Mazda, not Toyota times, and the range is narrow as a result; midsize uses an FCA warranty time for the Jeep Compass (0.9 hr) and a Kia warranty time for the Cadenza (1.0-1.3 hr), not a Camry; truck uses a parts seller's 1-hour figure for the F-150 itself and the same seller's 2-hour figure for the housing on a different F-150 engine, not book times; luxury uses a DIY guide's 'an hour or two' for the 328i's own engine, which covers the water pump as well. Warranty times are the low end of what shops bill, and bleeding air from the cooling system adds time on some cars.
extras: A quote almost always adds coolant (a top-up, or a full drain and refill) and time to bleed air from the cooling system, plus a new gasket or seal where it is not supplied with the thermostat (about $9 at Toyota list). Also common: a diagnosis fee for the overheating, no-heat or check-engine complaint (often code P0128), a new thermostat housing or water outlet where the plastic has warped or the thermostat only comes as a unit with it (about $55 aftermarket to $205 at Ford list on the F-150 listings seen), a coolant temperature sensor, radiator or heater hoses and clamps that are disturbed, a full coolant flush, shop supplies and sales tax. On some engines the shop will suggest doing the water pump at the same time because it sits behind the same parts.
